hints: Going faster never makes you arrive later. So among speeds 1 to 10<sup>7</sup>, the ones that work form a block at the top. What is the time formula for one speed — careful about the waiting rule for the last bus?
Binary search on the speed in [1, 107]. Time at speed s = Σ ceil(dist[i] / s) for every ride except the last, plus dist[last] / s as an exact fraction. If even 107 is too slow, answer -1.

1. Write time(s): integer ceil for the first n − 1 rides, then add dist[n-1] / (double) s.
  2. If time(107) > hour, return -1.
  3. lo = 1, hi = 107; while lo < hi take mid.
  4. If time(mid) <= hour, hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1.
  5. Return lo.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try speeds 1, 2, 3, ... up to 10<sup>7</sup> and return the first that arrives in time.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Binary search the smallest speed; each check walks the rides once.

explain: For dist = [4,2,6] and hour = 3.5: at speed 4, ride 1 takes 1 h, ride 2 takes 0.5 h but you wait until the next hour so it counts as 1, and the last ride takes 6/4 = 1.5 h with no waiting: 3.5 h total, on time. At speed 3 it is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 h, too slow, so 4 is the smallest. For hour = 1.9 with 3 rides it is impossible (the first two rides already need 2 whole hours), so the check at 107 fails and we return -1. Compare times with a tiny tolerance (1e-9) to avoid floating-point surprises.
recognize: 'Minimum integer speed so the total time stays within a limit' → binary search on the answer.
